content: 1. Watya et al. (2008) conducted a study in Rakai, Uganda, to evaluate the safety of adult male circumcision in both HIV-infected and uninfected men. The findings were published in PLoS Medicine. 2. Lagarde et al. (2009) investigated the high rate of adverse events following circumcision of young adult males using the Tara KLamp technique in South Africa. This randomized trial was detailed in the South African Medical Journal. 3. Kanyago et al. (2013) compared the Shang Ring device to the forceps-guided method for adult male circumcision in southwestern Uganda. This randomized controlled effectiveness study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 4. Mutabazi et al. (2012) conducted a prospective, randomized, non-masked trial comparing a non-surgical circumcision device to a surgical technique for HIV prevention in resource-limited settings. The study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 5. Sokal et al. (2014) performed a randomized controlled trial comparing the Shang Ring to conventional surgical techniques for adult male circumcision. The study focused on safety and acceptability and was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 6. Tshimanga et al. (2016) conducted a Phase II randomized controlled trial in Zimbabwe to compare the safety, procedure time, and cost of the PrePex device to forceps-guided surgical circumcision. The findings were published in PLoS One. 7. Kigozi et al. (2013) assessed the acceptability and safety of the Shang Ring for adult male circumcision in Rakai, Uganda. The results were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 8. Kigozi et al. (2014) evaluated the safety and acceptance of the PrePex device for non-surgical adult male circumcision in Rakai, Uganda, through a non-randomized observational study. The findings were published in PLoS One. 9. Millard et al. (2013) conducted a randomized trial on rapid, minimally invasive adult voluntary male circumcision. The study was published in the South African Medical Journal. 10. Millard et al. (2014) evaluated the Unicirc, a novel disposable device, in a randomized trial for rapid, minimally invasive adult voluntary male circumcision. The findings were published in the South African Medical Journal. 11. Kigozi et al. (2013) explored the acceptability and safety of the Shang Ring for adolescent male circumcision in Rakai, Uganda. The study was presented as an abstract (TUPE148). 12. Shenje and Millard (2016) conducted a randomized field trial of Unicirc, a single-use surgical instrument, for sutureless adult voluntary male circumcision with topical anesthetic. The study was published in PLoS One. 13. Ngo and Obhai (2012) examined male circumcision uptake, postoperative complications, and satisfaction associated with mid-level providers in rural Kenya. The findings were published in HIV AIDS (Auckland). 14. Phili et al. (2014) reported low adverse event rates following voluntary medical male circumcision in a high HIV burden public sector prevention program in South Africa. The study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 15. Brito et al. (2015) conducted a clinical trial to introduce voluntary medical male circumcision for HIV prevention in high-prevalence areas of the Dominican Republic. The findings were published in PLoS One. 16. Wirth et al. (2017) performed a prospective cohort study in Botswana to evaluate the safety and patient satisfaction of voluntary medical male circumcision. The study was published in PLoS One. 17. Hove et al. (2019) described the integration of voluntary medical male circumcision into traditional circumcision contexts in Zimbabwe, based on experiences of a local consortium collaborating with an ethnic group. The findings were published in Global Health: Science and Practice. 18. Buwembo et al. (2012) evaluated the safety and efficiency of the dorsal slit and sleeve methods of male circumcision performed by physicians and clinical officers in Rakai, Uganda. The study was published in BJU International. 19. Herman-Roloff et al. (2012) identified factors associated with the safety of voluntary medical male circumcision in Nyanza Province, Kenya. The findings were published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 20. Frajzyngier et al. (2014) assessed the safety of adult medical male circumcision performed by non-physician clinicians in Kenya through a prospective cohort study. The study was published in Global Health: Science and Practice. 21. Reed et al. (2015) evaluated loss-to-follow-up and postoperative adverse events in a voluntary medical male circumcision program in Nyanza Province, Kenya. The findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 22. Soboi et al. monitored adverse events in a new mature male circumcision client cohort in Namibia. The findings were presented as an abstract (WEPEC0909). 23. Muquingue et al. (2017) analyzed adverse events in a national voluntary medical male circumcision program in Mozambique from 2009 to 2017, noting reductions in adverse events with national scale-up but identifying three events requiring further attention. The findings were presented as an abstract (TUAC0204). 24. Bochner et al. (2017) described the adverse event profile of a mature voluntary medical male circumcision program performing PrePex and surgical procedures in Zimbabwe. The study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 25. Montague et al. (2014) implemented adolescent-friendly voluntary medical male circumcision using a school-based recruitment program in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The findings were published in PLoS One. 26. Kohler et al. (2016) classified and reported rates of adverse events in a Malawi male circumcision program, highlighting the impact of quality improvement training. The study was published in BMC Health Services Research. 27. Ngcobo et al. (2018) analyzed the quality of voluntary medical male circumcision performed by mid-level workers in Tshwane District, South Africa, through a retrospective analysis. The findings were published in PLoS One. 28. Lissouba et al. (2010) proposed a model for rolling out comprehensive adult male circumcision services in African low-income settings with high HIV incidence, based on the ANRS 12126 Bophelo Pele Project. The study was published in PLoS Medicine. 29. Hella et al. (2018) documented the transition from the forceps-guided to the dorsal slit technique in a voluntary medical male circumcision program in Tanzania. The findings were presented as a report. 30. Feldacker et al. (2018) examined the timing of adverse events among voluntary medical male circumcision clients in Zimbabwe, with implications for routine service delivery. The study was published in PLoS One.
